podcast.title: Lou Ottens' Engineering Career (1952-1986)
podcast.body: Lou Ottens joined Philips, the Dutch electronics company, as an engineer in 1952. By 1960, he was heading the company's new product development team. His dissatisfaction with "clunky user unfriendly reel-to-reel system[s]" led to his pivotal role in developing the compact cassette. He retired in 1986 and later acknowledged that his invention was obsolete but regretted that Sony, not Philips, introduced the revolutionary Walkman. Before retiring, he also worked on the compact disk. `"Lou Ottens worked for Phillips, the Dutch electronics company, first taking a job as an engineer in 1952. Eight years later, he headed up the company's new product development team."`

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Portable Music: Part 1

podcast.title: Compact Cassette Invention and Unveiling (1962-1963)
podcast.body: Lou Ottens and his team at Philips dramatically shrunk the reel-to-reel mechanism by 1962, encasing it in wood. The size (4x2.5x0.5 inches) was determined by a shirt pocket, with a 3.81mm wide tape (rounded to 4mm) divided into four tracks, running at 1 7/8 inches per second. Initially intended for office dictation, high fidelity was not a priority. The wooden prototype was replaced by plastic, and the "compact cassette" was unveiled at the Berlin Radio Show (Funko-Stellen) on August 30, 1963, promoted as "smaller than a pack of cigarettes." `"By 1962, he and his team had shrunk the reel-to-reel mechanism dramatically, encasing it in a wooden case."`

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Portable Music: Part 1

podcast.title: Compact Disc Naming (1963-1979)
podcast.body: The name "Compact Disc" was Philips' idea, inspired by their earlier invention, the "compact cassettes" in 1963. This name was agreed upon for the new format during the collaboration with Sony. "As for the name, well, that was Phillips idea. They invented the compact cassettes in 1963. That's what you actually call these things compact cassettes. So it was agreed that the new format should be called the compact disk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rise and Fall of the CD

podcast.title: Cassette Tape Invention and Patent (1964)
podcast.body: Philips was the company responsible for first introducing and patenting the cassette tape in 1964. However, its initial version suffered from very poor quality and high noise, which limited its use primarily to voice recordings and dictation rather than widespread musical applications. "fue en 1964 cuando Philis presentó el cassette y lo patentó."

podcast.title: Cassette Standardization (1965)
podcast.body: Despite initial competition from companies like Grundig and Telefunken, Philips' cassette design achieved global standardization after a 1965 licensing deal with Sony, which allowed Sony to use the design for free. This strategic move ensured Philips' design became the worldwide standard, leading to billions of cassettes being produced. `"It wasn't until Philips made a licensing deal with Sony in 1965, giving them the right to use the design for free, that things really began to take off."`

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Portable Music: Part 1

podcast.title: Initial Music Cassette Failure (1966)
podcast.body: In 1966, Philips introduced the first "musicassette" specifically intended for musical applications. Despite this, it proved to be an absolute market failure due to its high cost and persistently poor sound quality, which was not sufficient for general music consumption. "Al ser hizo algún lanzamiento pero fue un fracaso absoluto porque era bastante caro pero también su calidad era muy mala."

podcast.title: Cassette Patent Liberation (1971)
podcast.body: Philips eventually conceded to market pressures and, significantly influenced by Sony, decided to liberate the cassette patent in 1971. This crucial decision allowed other manufacturers, including Sony, to further develop and improve the cassette format, setting the stage for its later commercial success. "Al final Philips se rindió y en 1971 decidió liberar la patente, sobre todo para que Sony la presionaba, para que Sony pudiese manejar también en la cinta de cassette."

podcast.title: CD Development and Naming (1974-1979)
podcast.body: In 1974, a group of Philips engineers led by Lou Ottens began researching ways to improve vinyl records. They experimented with a 20-centimeter disk before settling on an 11.5-centimeter diameter, a size chosen because it matched the diagonal width of Philips' own compact cassette. In 1979, Philips teamed with Sony to develop the compact disk, contributing expertise in manufacturing processes and proposing the "compact disk" name, leveraging its prior success with the "compact cassette." `"In 1974, a group of engineers within Phillips led by Lou Ottens started to look for ways to improve on the vinyl record."`

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Portable Music: Part 1

podcast.title: Collaboration with Sony on CD Standards (1979)
podcast.body: Philips teamed up with Sony in 1979 after both companies realized they were working toward the same goal for a new music storage format. This collaboration involved splitting research costs, sharing knowledge, and establishing the proper standards, resulting in the "Red Book CDDA standard." "In 1979, when Sony and Phillips realized that they were working towards the same goal, the companies teamed up to split the costs of research, to share knowledge, and to come up with all the proper standards for making this new music storage format."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rise and Fall of the CD

podcast.title: Cassette Development (early 1960s)
podcast.body: Philips developed the compact cassette in the early 1960s. The diagonal width of these cassettes, 11.5 centimeters, influenced the initial diameter experiments for compact discs, with Philips' engineers first experimenting with 20 cm disks before settling on 11.5 cm. "Because Phillips also developed the cassette in the early 1960s. The diagonal width of a cassette is 11.5 centimeters."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rise and Fall of the CD

podcast.title: Co-developer of the Compact Disc (1970s)
podcast.body: Philips was a key titan in audiovisual culture during the 1970s, working jointly with Sony to develop the technology for the Compact Disc. Their collaboration focused on creating a new laser-reading system, laying the foundation for the digital audio format. "Se desarrolló prácticamente a medias entre Philips y Sony."

podcast.title: Collaboration with Sony on CD Technology
podcast.body: Philips, a Dutch company, worked with Sony for several years on the development of Compact Disk Technology. They released their own CD player, the CD100, about a month after Sony's CDP 101. "Sony had been working on Compact Disk Technology with a Dutch company called Phillips for a number of years, which released their own machine, the CD100, a bit of a month later."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rise and Fall of the CD

podcast.title: Financial Gains from CD Licensing Royalties
podcast.body: Philips, along with Sony, earned significant money from licensing royalties on the compact disc technology. Every CD sold contributed a small fee to the two companies, allowing them to clean up financially as CD sales skyrocketed. "1 billion in 1992, 2 billion in 1993, and Sony and Phillips cleaned up too. They made money from the licensing royalties of the technology. Every single CD, earned Sony and Phillips a little piece, a little taste, because of licensing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rise and Fall of the CD

podcast.title: Initial CD Manufacturing Plant in Germany
podcast.body: One of the two original compact disc manufacturing factories was run by Philips near Hanover, Germany, serving as a key production site for the new format. "Two factories were originally set up. Philips ran one near Hanover, Germany, and the other was run by Sony in Japan."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rise and Fall of the CD

podcast.title: Rejection of The Kinks
podcast.body: Philips was one of the record labels that "turned down" The Ravens (The Kinks), along with EMI and Decca, before the group found a home with Pye Records. "Philips also turned them down, which when the bid default ended up recording for Pie records."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 119: "You Really Got Me" by the Kinks

podcast.title: Rigorous Cassette Patent Impact
podcast.body: Philips' rigid patent system for the audio cassette significantly slowed its evolution and almost led to its failure. This experience influenced Sony and Philips' approach to the Compact Disc, leading them to adopt a more open licensing system to ensure widespread industry adoption. "La rigorosa patente que tenía Philips del sistema de cassette."

podcast.title: Sponsorship of Dire Straits Tour
podcast.body: Philips heavily promoted the compact disc format by sponsoring Dire Straits' tour for their digitally recorded album "Brothers in Arms." This sponsorship included Mark Knopfler appearing in a TV commercial to promote the CD, contributing to the album's success as the first CD to sell a million copies. "Phillips went so far as to sponsor DireStraight's Tour in support of their digitally recorded album Brothers and Arms. Leader Mark Knopfler even did a TV commercial, extolling the virtues of the CD."
